title: Synthetic data generation
summary: A model generates test inputs, and sometimes reference answers, from your documents or your agent's definition. It solves the cold start and widens coverage, but only after human review and with a tag that keeps it apart from real rows.
useIf: You have no traces yet, expert time is scarce, or you need more edge-case coverage than hand writing allows.
avoidIf: You plan to use unreviewed generated rows as the only evidence of quality, or to keep them after the prompt changed.

explain.md: In **synthetic data generation** an LLM reads a source and writes cases. Foundry offers two task types: **Simple QnA**, single turn with `query` and `ground_truth`, and **Simulation seed**, multi-turn scenarios described by `test_case_description`. Inputs can be an agent definition, an inline prompt or a reference file, and `max_samples` accepts 1 to 1,000 [[r8]].

Foundry's own practice advice is the checklist to follow: generate a small batch first and review the rows by hand, mirror the production system prompt, regenerate and version the dataset whenever instructions change, and combine synthetic with trace-derived data [[r8]]. RAGAS states the target as a dataset with high-quality samples, wide variety, enough rows for significant conclusions, and continual updates against drift [[tr4]].

steps.title: Generate small
steps.md: Ten to twenty rows from a document or agent definition.

steps.title: Review by hand
steps.md: Check the question is answerable and the reference is correct.

steps.title: Filter and dedupe
steps.md: Drop near duplicates and trivial rows. Add hard and multi-hop cases.

steps.title: Tag and version
steps.md: Mark `source: synthetic`, record the generator and prompt version.

steps.title: Scale and refresh
steps.md: Generate more once a reviewed sample is sound. Regenerate on prompt change.

explain.md: Mind three biases (reasoning, not a vendor claim). A question written from a chunk reuses that chunk's words, so lexical retrieval looks better than it will on real user wording. A generator from the same model family tends to write questions that model finds easy. And a generated reference can be wrong, which then punishes a correct system.

explain.title: Region support
explain.md: Synthetic data generation is supported only in a listed set of regions, for example East US 2, Sweden Central and West Europe, per the limits page checked on 2026-10-13 [[r37]]. Check before you plan on it.

whereToUse: Cold start before launch, when there are no traces
Coverage of edge cases and rare document types that hand writing would miss
Multi-turn simulation seeds for conversational agents
Stress cases built from a knowledge base after a large content update
Augmenting a small expert-labelled set, never replacing it

use: No traces exist or traffic is private
A reviewer can check a sample of rows
You can regenerate when instructions change
avoid: Using it as the only evidence for a high-harm launch
Skipping review because generation was cheap
Keeping stale rows after the system prompt changed
flips: Traces become available: shift weight to trace-mined rows and keep synthetic for gaps
Instructions or corpus change: regenerate and re-version
Rows are used to rank retrievers: add paraphrased and trace-style queries to reduce lexical overlap

pitfalls.symptom: Retrieval scores look excellent on synthetic rows and poor in production
pitfalls.cause: Questions were generated from the chunks and share their vocabulary
pitfalls.fix: Add paraphrased and trace-style queries, and judge retrieval on a held-out real slice

pitfalls.symptom: A correct system fails many synthetic rows
pitfalls.cause: The generated reference answer is wrong
pitfalls.fix: Review a sample, compute an error rate for the generator, and drop or correct bad rows

pitfalls.symptom: The agent behaves differently from what the dataset assumes
pitfalls.cause: The set was generated against an old system prompt
pitfalls.fix: Mirror the production prompt and regenerate and version the set on every instruction change

scenarios.title: New corpus, no users, one expert
scenarios.situation: A team indexes 5,000 product manuals for a support assistant. There is no traffic and one engineer who can review about 40 rows an hour.
constraints: Review capacity of about 40 rows an hour
unknowns: Is lexical overlap a risk for this corpus?
scenarios.question: How do you generate the first set?

options.name: Generate a small batch, review it, then scale with hard and multi-hop prompts and tag every row as synthetic
options.why: The review step measures the generator's error rate before volume, and tags keep synthetic apart from real data.
options.tradeoff: Review time up front and a quarterly regeneration chore.

options.name: Generate 3,000 rows and use them as-is
options.why: Unreviewed rows carry wrong references and easy questions, so scores are unreliable.
options.tradeoff: At volume it is fine only after a sampled review shows a low error rate.

options.name: Write 40 rows by hand and stop
options.tradeoff: Narrow coverage, and the set cannot detect small regressions.

flips.then: Add them and shrink the synthetic share.
Automate regeneration and review a rolling sample.

scenarios.title: Multi-turn agent, tool budget limited
scenarios.situation: A scheduling agent handles multi-turn conversations and calls booking tools. Real transcripts contain personal data, so no one will approve reuse for a few months.
constraints: Tool calls cost money in a sandbox
unknowns: Which intents and edge cases matter most?
Can tools run against a sandbox?
How are success and failure defined?
scenarios.question: How do you create test conversations?

options.name: Simulation seeds describing scenarios, reviewed, run against sandboxed tools with outcome checks
options.why: Seeds cover multi-turn flows without real PII, and outcome checks avoid judging fragile wording.
options.tradeoff: Simulated users are cleaner than real ones, so real transcripts remain the later target.

options.name: Single-turn question and answer rows only
options.why: They cannot exercise clarification, memory or tool sequences.
options.tradeoff: Right for a stateless lookup assistant.

flips.then: Mine them and use seeds for gaps.
Mock tool responses and grade the call arguments only.

scenarios.takeaway: For multi-turn agents, seed scenarios, not single questions.

quiz.q: Retrieval metrics are very high on generated questions but weak on real user queries. Most likely cause?
options: The embedding model is too small
The judge is biased toward long answers
Generated questions reuse the source chunks' wording, favouring lexical matching
quiz.explain: Questions written from a chunk echo its vocabulary, which flatters retrieval. Model size, judge length bias and a stale index are possible in general but do not explain this gap.

quiz.q: A reviewer checks 40 generated rows and finds 6 with a wrong reference. What is the sample error rate, in percent?
quiz.explain: 6 / 40 = 0.15, so 15%. With only 40 rows the interval is wide, but 15% is too high to scale without improving the generator prompt.

quiz.q: The production system prompt was rewritten last week. What should you do with the synthetic set?
options: Keep it, synthetic rows never go stale
Regenerate and version it against the new prompt
quiz.explain: Foundry advises mirroring the production prompt and regenerating when instructions change. The old set describes old behaviour.

flashcards.back: Simple QnA (single turn, query and ground_truth) and Simulation seed (multi-turn scenarios with test_case_description). max_samples accepts 1 to 1,000.

flashcards.front: Three bias risks of synthetic test data?
flashcards.back: Questions reuse chunk wording and flatter lexical retrieval, same-family generators write easy questions, and generated references can be wrong.

flashcards.front: When must synthetic rows be regenerated?
flashcards.back: Whenever the system instructions change. Review a small batch first and combine synthetic with trace-derived data.
